content.intro: This lesson covers Building, Checking, Running, and Testing Projects. It sits in Module 11, Modules, Crates, Packages, and Cargo, and builds toward a practical Rust mental model rather than memorizing a term in isolation.
content.why_it_matters: Building, Checking, Running, and Testing Projects matters when you work with repeatable quality checks and feedback. Understanding the rule helps you predict compiler or runtime behavior, document assumptions, and choose a safer implementation when inputs or system conditions change.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Reliable code uses tests and diagnostics to make assumptions visible. Unit tests isolate behavior, integration tests exercise public boundaries, and documentation tests keep example code checked alongside the API.

content_blocks.title: A reliable way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: For Building, Checking, Running, and Testing Projects, write down the inputs, the guarantee you expect, and the boundary where that guarantee stops. Work through a minimal example first; then deliberately test one edge case. Cargo.toml declares a package and dependency intent; Cargo.lock records a resolved graph for reproducible application builds. Keep module visibility deliberate.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not assume Building, Checking, Running, and Testing Projects guarantees more than it actually does. Reduce a failure to a small reproducer, read the full compiler diagnostic or error value, consult the matching official reference, and change one assumption at a time.

content_blocks.title: Toolchain and execution boundary
content_blocks.text: Course examples are static reference snippets, not executed inside CodeLeaf. Most standard-library examples can be tried in a Rust 2024 Cargo project; specialized networking, database, async, procedural-macro, embedded, and WebAssembly scenarios require the toolchain and dependencies described in their lessons.
